questions.title: What exactly is being rotated in Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT) when multiplying by $\mathbf{R}$ on the left?
questions.question_body: The paper says OFT optimizes an orthogonal matrix $\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ for a pretrained linear layer $\mathbf{W}^0\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ and changes the forward pass from $\mathbf{z}=(\mathbf{W}^0)^\top\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{z}=(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0)^\top\mathbf{x}$. I am confused about the geometric effect: does left-multiplying by $\mathbf{R}$ rotate the column vectors (neurons) of $\mathbf{W}^0$ or the row space? How does this preserve pairwise angles between neurons (columns) precisely? Could you show the algebraic identity that proves angle preservation?

questions.title: Why use the Cayley transform to parameterize orthogonal matrices and what are its limitations?
questions.question_body: The paper uses the Cayley parameterization $\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}$ with $\mathbf{Q}$ skew-symmetric. I know Cayley maps skew-symmetric matrices to orthogonal ones, but I have several confusions: (1) Why choose Cayley over the exponential map $\exp(\mathbf{S})$ with $\mathbf{S}$ skew-symmetric? (2) The Cayley transform is undefined if $\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q}$ is singular; under what conditions can that happen? (3) I read Cayley cannot represent orthogonal matrices with eigenvalue $-1$. How severe is that restriction in practice for finetuning?

questions.title: How is the claimed effective parameter count $\frac{1}{2}(b-1) d m$ for BOFT derived?
questions.question_body: The paper states BOFT($m,b$) takes $\frac{1}{2}(b-1) d m$ effective trainable parameters for a layer of size $d\times n$. I do not follow that derivation. What assumptions are used (e.g., per-block parameterization via skew-symmetric entries)? Please show a step-by-step counting of independent parameters in terms of $d$, $b$, and $m$ and explain what "effective" means here (why not just count all non-zero entries?).

questions.title: What is a block butterfly component $\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^b(d,k)$ and how exactly are its entries structured?
questions.question_body: The paper defines a block butterfly component $\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^b(d,k)$ where "each entry in $\mathbf{d}_i$ becomes a $b\times b$ matrix". I am having trouble visualizing this. Could you give a concrete small example, e.g. $d=8$, $k=2$, $b=2$, showing the block structure and the sizes of the matrices and indicate which blocks are nonzero vs zero?

questions.title: How do you ensure each butterfly component is orthogonal if its nonzeros are arranged as in Equation (1)?
questions.question_body: Equation (1) defines a butterfly factor $\mathbf{B}^F(k)$ as a $2\times 2$ block matrix with diagonal blocks being diagonal matrices $\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{d}_i)$. The paper then says we can guarantee orthogonality by applying Cayley transform to $2\times2$ blocks. I'm confused: how do we parameterize the diagonal entries $\mathbf{d}_i$ to make the whole $\mathbf{B}^F(k)$ orthogonal? Is orthogonality enforced per $2\times 2$ sub-block, per scalar, or via some permutation? Please give the exact parameterization used to make each butterfly component orthogonal.

questions.title: Why does BOFT reduce to block-diagonal OFT when $m=1$ and to full OFT when $m=1,b=d$?
questions.question_body: The paper asserts BOFT($1,b$) reduces to block-diagonal OFT with block size $b$, and BOFT($1,d$) reduces to the original (full) OFT. I don't fully see the connection between the product-of-butterfly-components formulation and a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix. Could you explain how the product collapses into a single block-diagonal matrix when $m=1$ and how choosing $b=d$ recovers an unconstrained dense orthogonal matrix?

questions.title: How does the information transmission graph correspond to nonzero entries in the matrix product $\mathbf{R}=\prod_{i=1}^m \mathbf{B}_i$?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces a grid graph of $d\times(m+1)$ nodes and says a directed edge between adjacent levels corresponds to a nonzero element in a factor $\mathbf{B}_i$. I want to be precise: given adjacency matrices $A_i$ (nonzero pattern of $\mathbf{B}_i$), why does existence of a path from source node $j$ to sink node $i$ correspond exactly to $R_{ij}\neq 0$? Are we assuming no cancellation can make the sum zero? If entries have real values, can't sums cancel and yield zeros even if paths exist?

questions.title: Why are $d$ edges between adjacent levels considered "non-trainable" because they must be $\pm 1$ for orthogonality?
questions.question_body: The information transmission section says an orthogonal factor needs at least $d$ edges to be bijection and that these edges shouldn't be counted because they are not trainable (e.g., for a $d\times d$ orthogonal with $d$ non-zero entries, those entries can only be $\pm1$). I don't understand this claim: is it always true that a sparse orthogonal matrix with exactly $d$ nonzeros must be a permutation matrix with entries $\pm1$? If so, why? Please clarify the logic and give a small counterexample if the claim is not generally true.

questions.title: How does BOFT handle dimensions $d$ that are not powers of two?
questions.question_body: The butterfly construction is presented assuming $d=2^N$. In practice many model hidden sizes are not powers of two (e.g., 3072, 4096 etc.). What practical strategies do the authors propose: (a) pad to the next power of two, (b) use mixed radix butterflies, (c) custom permutations? What are the trade-offs of these options and how do they affect orthogonality and parameter counts?

questions.title: What are the computational costs (FLOPs) of BOFT during training compared to OFT and LoRA?
questions.question_body: BOFT composes $\mathbf{R}$ as a product of $m$ sparse orthogonal factors. Intuitively parameter count is lower (e.g., $O(d\log d)$), but each forward/backward requires applying $m$ factors. Could you provide the asymptotic FLOP count for computing $\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0$ (or applying $\mathbf{R}$ to a vector) in BOFT versus dense OFT and LoRA? Also, how does the wall-clock training time compare empirically?

questions.title: How expressive is a single butterfly matrix versus a product of butterfly matrices?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 says BOFT is more expressive than OFT with the same block size and that a product of many butterfly matrices can approximate all orthogonal matrices. I am confused about the difference: (a) How much of the orthogonal group can a single butterfly matrix (the standard Cooley–Tukey pattern) represent? (b) Why do we need multiple (maybe $\Theta(d)$) products to reach full expressivity? A short proof sketch or intuition would help.

questions.title: In the expressivity experiment approximating a random orthogonal matrix, what loss and optimization details were used?
questions.question_body: Figure 4 (referenced in the text) evaluates approximation error of BOFT variants approximating a random $512\times512$ orthogonal matrix. I want to reproduce this experiment: what is the optimization objective (e.g., minimize Frobenius norm $\|\hat{R}-R_{target}\|_F^2$?), what optimizer, learning rate, initialization, number of steps/epochs, and do they optimize over permutation choices? Also how is "approximation error" measured exactly?

questions.title: How does multiplicative Dropout work and why is it needed instead of standard Dropout?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces a "multiplicative Dropout" that randomly picks $p_1$ percent of butterfly components and $p_2$ percent of diagonal blocks in each component and replaces these blocks with identity matrices. I have several questions: (1) Why can't standard additive Dropout or DropConnect be applied here? (2) When you replace blocks by identity, won't that break orthogonality of the component (or does identity preserve it)? (3) What are recommended values of $p_1,p_2$ and how sensitive are results?

questions.title: What does the paper mean by "effective" trainable parameters when counting edges in the information transmission graph?
questions.question_body: Throughout the paper they sometimes count the number of edges and call them effective parameters, but also point out some orthogonality constraints make some edges non-trainable or dependent. Could you clarify the distinction between raw nonzero entries, degrees of freedom under orthogonality, and the notion of "effective" trainable parameters in this framework?

questions.title: How do you choose $(m,b)$ for BOFT in practice given a parameter budget?
questions.question_body: BOFT has two hyperparameters: depth $m$ (number of butterfly components) and block size $b$. The paper states trade-offs (smaller $b$, larger $m$ more parameter-efficient) but gives no recipe. Given a target budget of $P$ parameters for a layer of size $d$, how should I choose $m$ and $b$ to (a) meet the budget and (b) maximize expressivity? Is there a simple algebraic rule or search strategy?

questions.title: How does BOFT interact with non-square weight matrices (e.g., attention projection $W\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times 4d}$)?
questions.question_body: The formulation uses $\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ multiplied on the left of $\mathbf{W}^0\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$. For many transformer layers $n\neq d$ (e.g., query/key/value or FFN matrices), is BOFT always applied as a left orthogonal transform of size $d$? What about cases where finetuning might want to act on the output dimension (right-multiplication) or both sides—does BOFT generalize to those?

questions.title: What numerical stability or conditioning issues arise from composing many orthogonal butterfly factors?
questions.question_body: Composing many orthogonal matrices is still orthogonal, but numerical errors can accumulate in finite precision. Are there observed stability issues with backpropagating through many Cayley parameterized small blocks and multiplying them together? Does the Cayley parameterization alleviate/introduce conditioning issues compared to parameterizing the full orthogonal matrix directly?

questions.title: Why does BOFT give better generalization inductive bias than block-diagonal OFT?
questions.question_body: The authors claim butterfly structure "recovers many classic linear transforms" and provides a smoother interpolation between identity and the full orthogonal group, implying better inductive bias. I am struggling to understand the concrete reason: can you give an intuitive example or a toy task where block-diagonal OFT fails but BOFT succeeds, and link that to which inductive biases each imposes?

questions.title: How does BOFT compare empirically to LoRA when both are given the same parameter budget?
questions.question_body: LoRA is a popular low-rank additive adapter. The paper claims orthogonal finetuning (BOFT) outperforms SOTA methods. But I want a focused comparison: for a fixed parameter budget (e.g., 1M trainable params) and a given layer shape, how do BOFT and LoRA compare in (a) task accuracy, (b) training stability, (c) wall-clock training time? If the paper doesn't report this, what would you expect and why?

questions.title: How does the BOFT parameterization handle permutation matrices and permutations between butterfly layers?
questions.question_body: Butterfly factorizations often include permutations between stages (bit-reversal, etc.). The paper mentions permutations but does not fully specify them. Are permutations learned as part of the parameters, are they fixed pre-specified permutations (e.g., FFT-style), or is there a learned reordering applied between butterfly components? How important are these permutations for expressivity?

questions.title: Does the Cayley transform applied to small $2b\times2b$ blocks represent all orthogonal matrices of that block size?
questions.question_body: The paper enforces orthogonality per $2b\times2b$ block by Cayley transform. For a single $2b\times2b$ orthogonal block, does Cayley parameterization cover the entire $O(2b)$ group (all orthogonal matrices) or only a subset (e.g., excluding matrices with eigenvalue $-1$)? If it's a subset, how does that restriction affect overall expressivity when composing many such blocks?

questions.title: How does BOFT ensure the product of block-orthogonal butterfly components yields a dense matrix?
questions.question_body: I see the information transmission argument: if the concatenated graph connects every source to every sink then the product is dense in nonzero pattern. But given we enforce orthogonality per component with structured sparsity, how do we guarantee that the product has no accidental zero entries (due to cancellations) or structural zeros? Is there a combinatorial condition that guarantees a fully dense pattern irrespective of values?

questions.title: Why is preserving the spectral norm of $\mathbf{W}^0$ beneficial for training stability?
questions.question_body: The paper claims orthogonal finetuning preserves the spectral norm because left-multiplying by an orthogonal matrix doesn't change singular values. How does this preservation concretely help training stability or generalization? Are there theoretical results or intuitive arguments (e.g., gradient norms, Lipschitz constants) that explain why maintaining spectral norm is helpful?

questions.title: Is there a provable lower bound on number of butterfly stages $m$ needed to approximate an arbitrary orthogonal matrix to given accuracy?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 indicates a product of many butterfly matrices can represent the whole orthogonal group, but it doesn't give how many are needed. Is there any known lower/upper bound on $m$ (as a function of $d$ and approximation tolerance $\epsilon$) required to approximate any orthogonal matrix within error $\epsilon$? If not exact, are there empirical guidelines?

questions.title: How to implement BOFT efficiently in PyTorch/TensorFlow to avoid dense $d\times d$ matmuls?
questions.question_body: From an implementation standpoint, we want to exploit the sparse factorization and avoid constructing $\mathbf{R}$ explicitly. Do you multiply the small blocks sequentially into $\mathbf{W}^0$ (i.e., apply each sparse factor to $\mathbf{W}^0$ in order)? Are there efficient kernels for the butterfly pattern? Any tips to keep GPU memory/compute efficient and not to materialize dense $d\times d$ matrices during forward/backward?

questions.title: How does BOFT interact with optimizer states and parameter freezing in large models?
questions.question_body: In PEFT, one advantage is only storing optimizer states for few trainable params. For BOFT, the parameters live in many small blocks across layers. Does this create fragmentation that impacts optimizer memory or performance? Any practical considerations (e.g., grouping parameters, using fused optimizers) to keep memory overhead low?

questions.title: Can you give an intuition/short proof why a product like $\mathbf{B}_{d-1,1}\mathbf{B}_{d-1,2}^\top\cdots\mathbf{B}_{1,1}\mathbf{B}_{1,2}^\top$ spans the entire orthogonal group as claimed in Theorem 1?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 asserts that multiplying a sequence of butterfly matrices and their transposes can approximate any orthogonal matrix. I want a short, intuitive explanation (or pointer to a reference like kaleidoscope hierarchy) of why alternating products of fast-transform-like sparse factors can generate the full orthogonal group. Where does the argument come from?
